abstract: Pluripotent cells exist as a continuum during early development and are characterized by their capacity to differentiate into all embryonic lineages. While this concept was initially defined based on the behaviour of mammalian pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) in vitro, pluripotency is essential for the construction of complex body plans across the animal kingdom through the generation of diverse cell types. In vitro, PSCs can be captured in discrete states as embryonic stem cells or through cellular reprogramming to generate induced pluripotent stem cells. These in vitro tools have proven central to dissecting the molecular basis of pluripotency amongst eutherian mammalian models and beyond. Here, we consider the evolution of pluripotency through the lens of lineage specification across the animal kingdom. We first chart the progression of pluripotent cell populations from zygote to gastrulation across amniote and anamniote taxa, framing these transitions against the Developmental Hourglass Model. We then examine how the core pluripotency network, namely the POU5-SOXB1-NANOG/VENTX autoregulatory loop, is conserved across jawed vertebrates and how whole-genome duplication events shaped the paralogue diversity of its components. We further consider the evolutionary roots of this network and suggest that the antagonism between self-renewal and differentiation is a fundamental property conserved throughout the animal kingdom, the governing transcription factor network of which has been continually refined through the evolutionary tree. Together, the comparative perspective presented in this Review highlights both the evolutionary significance of pluripotency and the regulatory mechanisms governing developmental processes across diverse species.
